title: Letters Kept in Order
statement:
You get two strings, s and t. Return true if you can get s by deleting some characters of t (possibly none) without changing the order of the rest. Otherwise return false.

The kept characters do not have to be next to each other in t. An empty s can always be made.

examples.why: All three letters are in "spoken", but n comes last there. Containing the letters is not enough; the order must match.

hints: Match the first letter of s. Is there ever a reason to match it to a later copy in t than the first one you find?
Taking the earliest match leaves the most of t for the remaining letters, so greedy is safe.
Two indexes: i in s, j in t. Move j every step; move i only when s[i] === t[j]. At the end, check whether i reached the end of s.

explain.intuition:
Walk through t once, and keep a finger on the next letter of s you still need. Each time t shows that letter, take it and move the finger forward. If the finger gets past the end of s, all its letters were found in order.

Why is grabbing the first match always safe? Matching a letter as early as possible leaves the longest possible rest of t for the remaining letters. Any solution that uses a later copy could switch to the earlier one and still work. That exchange argument is what makes the greedy two-pointer scan correct.
steps: Go through each character of t. If i < s.length and the character equals s[i], increase i.
pitfalls: Only checking that every letter of s appears in t. Order matters: "nep" is not inside "spoken".
Looking for s as a contiguous substring. The kept letters may have gaps.
Forgetting repeated letters: "aa" needs two separate a's in t.

solutions.title: Two pointers
solutions.idea: Scan t once and advance in s on every match. Greedy earliest matches are always safe.

solutions.title: Positions per letter plus binary search
solutions.idea: Precompute where each letter occurs in t. For each letter of s, binary search the first occurrence after the previous match. Worth it when many strings s are checked against the same t.

followups: A billion strings s are checked against the same long t. What do you precompute so each check is fast?
Count how many different ways s can be picked out of t.
